title: Is Wool Carpet Worth the Price? Pros and Cons for Seattle Homes
meta: Wool carpet is worth it in a Seattle bedroom or living room you will keep for decades, and a poor buy for pets, stairs and rentals. Wills Flooring weighs it.
keywords: is wool carpet worth it, wool carpet pros and cons, wool vs nylon carpet Seattle, wool carpet moths Pacific Northwest, best carpet for Seattle homes

blocks.lead: Wool carpet is worth the price in a Seattle bedroom, living room or formal space you plan to keep for 20 years, where nobody is tracking in mud and no pet is having accidents. It is not worth it on stairs, in a rental, in a basement, or anywhere a dog or toddler spends the day.
blocks.detail: Wool costs several times what a mid-grade nylon costs per square yard, and it earns that back only through longevity and feel. Wills Flooring brings wool, wool blends and the best synthetics to your Seattle home so you can compare them under your own feet, and prices every carpet job on site.

blocks.html: Wool comes up in Seattle more than almost anywhere else we work. Queen Anne and Capitol Hill homeowners restoring a 1920s house want the material the house was built with. Magnolia and Wallingford families want something natural in the bedrooms. And everyone who has priced it has the same follow-up: is it really that much better? The honest answer is that wool is better at some things and clearly worse at others. Here is the full list, with no salesmanship either way.

blocks.text: What wool does better than any synthetic

items.title: Resilience
items.text: Wool fibers are naturally crimped and spring back after furniture and foot traffic. A 15-year-old wool carpet in a Seattle living room often still looks full where a polyester of the same age has matted flat in the walk paths.

items.title: Moisture regulation
items.text: Wool absorbs and releases humidity without feeling damp, which matters in a city that spends eight months a year above 70 percent outdoor humidity. It takes the clammy edge off a bedroom in November.

items.title: Natural flame resistance
items.text: Wool is hard to ignite and self-extinguishes, which is why it is used in aircraft and hotels. No added chemistry is needed to get there.

items.title: Depth of color
items.text: Wool takes dye deep into the fiber and reads richer and more matte than synthetics. In the flat light of a Seattle winter, that softness is the thing people notice when they walk in.

items.title: Low VOC and biodegradable
items.text: Wool is sheared, spun and dyed. There is no petroleum in the fiber, and a wool carpet with a natural backing gives off very little odor in a new install.

items.title: Right for the house
items.text: Craftsman and Tudor homes in Ballard and Queen Anne were carpeted in wool originally. For a period-correct restoration, nothing else looks the same.

blocks.text: Wool vs wool blend vs nylon for Seattle rooms

a.title: Choose it for
items: Living and formal rooms in older Seattle homes
A home office where you sit and think, not where a dog sleeps
Condos in Capitol Hill or Belltown where sound and feel matter and traffic is light

b.title: Choose it for
items: Any room with a dog or cat
Rentals and homes you plan to sell within a few years

blocks.html: Wool blends, usually 80 percent wool and 20 percent nylon, are the compromise most Seattle families land on. The nylon adds abrasion resistance on the wear points, the wool still gives the look and hand, and the price sits in between. If you are choosing between fibers for the whole house, our fiber comparison goes deeper on each one.

blocks.text: What drives the price of a wool carpet job

items.text: 100 percent New Zealand wool in a dense loop or cut pile is the top. Blends and lighter face weights bring the material cost down a lot.
Wool is often woven narrower than synthetics, so seams and waste change with the room. A 12 by 14 Seattle bedroom cuts cleanly; an L-shaped living room does not.
Stairs are priced per step and are the most labor-intensive part of any carpet job. With wool we usually suggest a matching nylon or a runner on the stairs instead.
Wool deserves a dense pad. A cheap pad lets the backing flex and shortens the life of an expensive carpet.
Old carpet removal, stairs to a third floor and Seattle parking or elevator logistics are all quoted at the estimate.

blocks.text: When wool is the wrong buy

blocks.title: Be honest about your household:
blocks.text: If you have a dog under two, a cat with a history, a toddler, or a basement family room in a West Seattle or Beacon Hill home with any moisture history, wool will disappoint you. The stain and odor risk is not worth the fiber's other virtues, and a good nylon will look better in five years. We would rather sell you the right carpet than the expensive one.

items.html: Pets that have accidents. Urine bonds with wool protein. Unlike solution-dyed nylon, it usually cannot be fully cleaned out.
Basements and slab rooms. Wool plus a damp slab equals odor and, eventually, mildew.
Rentals and short holds. You will not get the 20-year payoff, and a buyer will not pay you back for it.
Sunrooms and big south windows. Fade is permanent.
A tight whole-house budget. Wool in every room usually means a thinner wool everywhere. Better: wool in two rooms, quality nylon in the rest.

blocks.text: How to buy wool carpet well in Seattle

items: Ask for the wool percentage, the face weight and whether the wool is moth-treated. All three are on the spec sheet.
See it in your own light. Wool's color shifts more than synthetics between showroom LEDs and a gray Seattle afternoon, which is why we bring samples to the house.
Put a full-size sample on the floor for a day and walk on it in socks. The hand of wool is the reason to buy it; make sure you like it.
Pair it with a dense pad and get the pad spec in writing.
Plan the stairs separately. A matching nylon or a bound wool runner over hardwood stairs saves the wool where it would wear.
Book a cleaner who advertises wool experience before you need one, and vacuum with suction only, no beater bar.
Get a written quote that lists carpet, pad, removal, stairs and seams as separate lines from an installer who will stand behind the seams with a workmanship warranty.

faq.q: Is wool carpet really worth the extra money?
faq.a: In the right room, yes. Wool holds its pile and color for 20 years or more, feels better underfoot and regulates humidity in a damp Seattle house. In a room with pets, kids or heavy traffic, the extra money buys problems, and a good nylon is the smarter spend.

faq.q: Does wool carpet have problems with moths in Seattle?
faq.a: It can. Clothes moths and carpet beetles like undisturbed wool, typically under furniture that never moves and along closet edges. Most quality wool carpet is moth-treated at the mill. Regular vacuuming of edges and under furniture keeps it from becoming an issue.

faq.q: Is wool carpet good for people with allergies?
faq.a: Generally yes. Wool is a natural fiber that traps dust until it is vacuumed rather than releasing it, gives off very little odor when new, and resists dust mites better than many synthetics because it stays drier. People with a true wool sensitivity should test a sample first.

faq.q: Can wool carpet go on stairs?
faq.a: It can, but it wears at the nosings faster than nylon on a busy stair. In most Seattle homes we suggest a matching nylon for the stairs or a bound wool runner that can be replaced separately. Stairs are priced per step at the estimate either way.

faq.q: How do I clean wool carpet?
faq.a: Vacuum with suction only or a gentle brush setting, blot spills immediately with water and a wool-safe cleaner, and hire a professional who works with wool for periodic cleaning. Over-wetting, alkaline cleaners and steam-heavy rental machines can brown, shrink or felt the fiber.

faq.q: What is a wool blend carpet?
faq.a: Usually 80 percent wool and 20 percent nylon. The nylon adds abrasion resistance where feet turn, while the wool still provides the look, softness and moisture handling. Blends cost less than pure wool and are the most common wool choice for Seattle families.
